rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention window and resolutions will guide subsequent narrowing and slope or temperature tests.
Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while measuring the critical pair's sensitivity to slope.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the full-resolution boundary. The critical pair is near the threshold at 8 minutes, so retain injection 2 as the faster maximum-CRF fallback if resolution drops.

Test whether higher temperature changes selectivity enough to resolve the critical pair at the shorter gradient. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect while potentially shortening retention further.
Test the lower temperature endpoint to map selectivity at the six-minute gradient, since 60 C introduced additional critical pairs. Injection 2 remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shorter gradient to seek a faster separation with altered selectivity. The early peaks were well retained at 40 C, providing room to raise phi0; injection 2 remains the maximum-CRF fallback.

Reduce the slope to match the fully resolved eight-minute gradient while retaining the higher starting organic fraction for speed. The previous last peak exited near 0.57 organic, so a 0.65 endpoint should provide adequate elution strength.
Raise temperature moderately to improve the critical middle-pair selectivity and shorten retention. At 50 C, the early pair may retain adequate separation without the near-coelution observed at 60 C.
Make the gradient one step shallower to lift the middle pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the early-pair separation. This should provide a faster maximum-CRF method than injection 2.

Explore whether a much steeper gradient separates the middle pair again after an elution-order reversal, with lower temperature protecting the early pair. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Return to the fully resolved shallow-gradient region, raising phi0 to shorten retention while narrowing the gradient to protect the middle pair. Lowering temperature slightly should help preserve early-pair separation at the higher starting organic fraction.

Increase temperature one step to try to bring the middle pair above R = 1.5 while shortening retention. The early pair has some resolution margin at 45 C, making this a targeted refinement of injection 11.

Test a hotter, steeper gradient for faster elution, lowering phi0 to help protect the early pair. This probes whether temperature can preserve middle-pair resolution at higher slope; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to shorten the initial retention while preserving middle-pair separation. Returning to 40 C should help protect the early pair from compression at the higher phi0.

Test the fast-gradient, reversed-selectivity region at a higher phi0, which may separate the middle pair on the opposite side of its coelution point. A moderate temperature should balance early- and late-pair resolution; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Refine the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method with a one-step shallower gradient to increase its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. The strong endpoint should still elute all compounds promptly, providing a more robust alternative to injection 12.

Explore whether a higher starting organic fraction at low temperature produces a useful alternative middle-pair selectivity while retaining the early compounds. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, so this is an exploratory test rather than a replacement.

Use a slope between injections 8 and 9 to target full middle-pair resolution with less retention than injection 9. The early pair should retain adequate separation, providing another fast maximum-CRF candidate.

Test a cooler neighbor of injection 16 to increase early-pair separation while retaining the middle-pair margin supplied by the shallower gradient. This seeks another maximum-CRF method with more balanced resolution margins.

Lower the temperature one step from injection 13 to restore early-pair resolution, testing whether its middle pair remains above 1.5. This targets another short, fully resolved method near the established selectivity boundary.

This grid combination makes the slope slightly steeper than injection 12, potentially shortening last-peak retention while preserving full resolution. It tests the nearby speed boundary; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF fallback.

Test a cooler neighbor of injection 9 to improve early-pair separation while retaining sufficient middle-pair resolution. With the maximum CRF already achieved, this refinement checks for a well-balanced fully resolved alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed option.

Preserve injection 9's slope through the critical middle pair, then switch to a hold using the minimum programmed gradient duration. This tests whether the late peaks can still elute promptly and remain resolved at a lower endpoint.

Refine injection 9 with a one-step shallower gradient to increase the middle-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes. This targets a maximum-CRF alternative with greater separation margin; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a slope between injections 12 and 16 to gain middle-pair resolution margin with only a small retention-time increase over injection 12. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
